newsitem.title: USA: U.S. withholds judgment on Cuba-Canada.
newsitem.headline: U.S. withholds judgment on Cuba-Canada.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday withheld judgment on an expected joint declaration by Canada and Cuba but expressed doubt that Havana would take meaningful steps toward establishing democratic rule.

"The United States remains sceptical that the Cuban government is in fact prepared to take systematic and meaningful steps that would lead toward ... a transition to democratic rule in Cuba. Or (steps) that would reflect a change in the position of the Cuban government on human rights," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
He followed Canada's lead in playing down a potential dispute with the United States over a visit by Ottawa's foreign minister, Lloyd Axworthy, to the communist-ruled island.

Whereas Burns on Tuesday said the Axworthy visit would "reward" Cuban President Fidel Castro, on Wednesday he said "the United States is not questioning the wisdom of this trip." Burns accused the media of playing up U.S.-Canada differences over Cuba.
"We're not even commenting on whether or not Minister Axworthy should have undertaken it. That's a decision for him and for the Canadian government," Burns said.
He said he called the Canadian Embassy in Washington to "explain" his remarks about rewarding Castro at Tuesday's news briefing, fearing they were misunderstood by reporters.

Axworthy met Castro in Havana on Tuesday and said Canada was making some progress in its policy of dialogue with Cuba. It was the highest level visit to the island by a Canadian official in two decades.

Axworthy said he raised issues like human rights and political prisoners with Castro, but did not give details. He was working on a joint declaration for future cooperation with Cuba in a range of areas that were expected to include human rights and governance.
Burns, asked about the declaration, said: "We'll look at it very closely, and if appropriate, have something to say perhaps tomorrow, if that's appropriate."

Washington considers it "a very good thing" that Axworthy is raising human rights in his Cuba talks but even in the past two weeks, Havana has continued oppressing its citizens, arresting several prominent democracy activists, he said.
"This reflects a continuing pattern of repression in Cuba by the Castro government which concerns us deeply ...(and) we urge the Cuban government to release them," he said.

Canada believes it can best encourage political and economic reform on the island through constructive engagement. Washington has long sought to isolate Cuba and last year toughened its 35-year-old economic embargo with its Helms-Burton law, which includes penalties on some third country firms doing business with Cuba. Ottawa has been a leading opponent of the law.
Burns also went out of his way not to get into a controversy over Pope John Paul II's plans to visit Cuba in 1998.

"We have the highest respect for the Pope ...He's shown his commitment to human rights and democracy all over the world beginning in his native Poland. So there is no reason for us to question in any way his intentions to travel to Cuba," the spokesman said.
